newsitem.title: USA: Enron sees electric retailing on horizon.
newsitem.headline: Enron sees electric retailing on horizon.

text.p: The head of Enron Corp's power marketing operation on Wednesday said open competition in U.S. electric retail markets could begin within three years in some parts of the country, much quicker than earlier expected.

Regulators are poised to topple electric utility monopoly controls in New England and California starting in January 1998, and regulations protecting monopolies in neighboring states should fall like dominoes by the turn of the century.
"I cannot tell you how quickly this process is moving," Skilling said at a standing-room only Houston conference on energy derivatives trading. "This is breakneck pace."

Legislators and regulators in 42 states are considering options for ending utility monopoly control over retail electric sales, while federal regulators are working to open regional transmission grids to competition, Skilling said.

Massachusetts and California are set to open their markets to retail competition on January 1, 1998, allowing consumers to select their electric companies much like they can now choose a long-distance telephone company, Skilling said.
Neighboring states in New England and the Pacific Northwest will quickly follow suit, and competition will spread quickly down the East and West Coasts, he said.

"Once that ball starts rolling down the hill, it is going to be very, very hard to stop," said Skilling, chairman of Enron Capital and Trade Resources, the Houston-based company's electricity and natural gas trading arm.

Enron has been leading the charge in wholesale electric sales, ranking second behind the Tennessee Valley Authority in megawatt hours sold. In the fourth quarter, Enron Capital will move about 20 million megawatt hours, Skilling said.
Its $2.1 billion acquisition of Portland General Corp gave Enron control of more than 5,900 megawatts of generating capacity, making it the seventh largest seller of electricity.

The company controls more than 30 percent of the non-regulated U.S. wholesale electric market, and has set a goal of capturing a 15 percent market share of the $144 billion a year domestic electric retail market once it is opened to competition.
"We think sometime in mid-1997, we will become the largest seller of power in North America," Skilling said of Enron Capital, a major player in the U.S. electric and gas markets.

Enron is in the running to manage peak power needs for Oglethorpe Power Corp, a Georgia cooperative which yesterday awarded a contract valued at up to $5 billion to an LG&E Energy Corp unit to manage its 3,200 megawatt generating capacity.
That contract has been seen as a blueprint for electric wholesalers building nationwide retail franchises.
